intro: Giving verbs have two settings: direction and level. First decide the direction exactly as with the plain verbs (outward, toward me, or I receive), then set the level. When the other person ranks above you (teacher, boss, customer, someone else's parent), each plain verb has a polite twin: あげる becomes さしあげる, くれる becomes くださる, もらう becomes いただく. One step below あげる sits やる, for animals, plants and your own juniors. The direction never changes when the level does.

skills.rule: When you or your side give something to someone you respect, use さしあげる.
skills.explain:
さしあげる is the humble version of あげる: same direction (from my side outward), same particles (giver は/が, receiver に, thing を). It lowers the giver to raise the receiver, so the receiver must be someone you show respect to: a teacher, your boss, a customer, a guest.

It only ever moves away from you. If a respected person gives to you, the verb is くださる; if you are the subject receiving, it is いただく.

The edge to know: ～てさしあげる (doing a favour for a superior) is grammatical, but said to that person's face it stresses that you are doing them a favour and sounds presumptuous. When offering help to a superior, use the humble お～する instead: お持ちします, ご案内します. Keep さしあげる for handing over things, and for reporting favours to a third person.
patterns: [I / my side] は [superior] に [thing] を さしあげる
[superior] に [thing] を さしあげてください (instructing staff)

examples.jp: 先生[せんせい]に花[はな]を{さしあげました}。
examples.en: I gave my teacher some flowers.

examples.jp: 社長[しゃちょう]に旅行[りょこう]のお土産[みやげ]を{さしあげました}。
examples.en: I gave the company president a souvenir from my trip.

examples.jp: お客様[きゃくさま]に新[あたら]しいカタログを{さしあげて}ください。
examples.en: Please give the customer the new catalogue.

examples.jp: 先生[せんせい]の退職[たいしょく]のお祝[いわ]いに、クラスで時計[とけい]を{さしあげました}。
examples.en: Our class gave the teacher a watch to celebrate their retirement.

contrast.note: Same direction, plain level. Fine for friends and equals; toward a teacher or boss it is too casual in polite speech.
The opposite direction: the respected person gives to me or my side.
The receiver is the subject: 先生にいただいた means I received it from the teacher.

mistakes.bad: 先生[せんせい]が私[わたし]に辞書[じしょ]を{さしあげました}。
mistakes.good: 先生[せんせい]が私[わたし]に辞書[じしょ]を{くださいました}。
mistakes.note: さしあげる moves away from me. When the teacher gives to me, use くださる.

mistakes.bad: 部長[ぶちょう]、お荷物[にもつ]を持[も]って{さしあげます}。
mistakes.good: 部長[ぶちょう]、お荷物[にもつ]を{お持[も]ちします}。
mistakes.note: Offering a favour to a superior's face with てさしあげる sounds presumptuous; use humble お～します.

skills.tip: さしあげる = 'hold up and offer'. The arrow starts at me and points up.

skills.rule: When someone you respect gives something to you or your side, use くださる.
skills.explain:
くださる is the honorific version of くれる: same direction (toward me or my in-group), same particles. The giver is the subject, marked が or は, and the receiver (私, 母, うちの子) is usually left out because it is obvious.

Its polite form is irregular: くださいます, not くださります. The request word ください is the imperative of this verb. With a て-form, ～てくださる means a respected person did something for me: 先生が説明してくださった.

The edge: くださる needs the receiver to be me or someone on my side. If a teacher gives something to another student who is not in your group, you are not receiving anything, so くださる does not fit. The same event seen from my side as the subject is いただく: 先生がくださった = 先生にいただいた.
patterns: [superior] が (私に) [thing] を くださる

examples.jp: 先生[せんせい]が辞書[じしょ]を{くださいました}。
examples.en: My teacher gave me a dictionary.

examples.jp: 部長[ぶちょう]がお菓子[かし]を{くださいました}。
examples.en: The department manager gave us some sweets.

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さんのお母[かあ]さんが手紙[てがみ]を{くださいました}。
examples.en: Tanaka-san's mother sent me a letter.

examples.jp: 先生[せんせい]が作文[さくぶん]を直[なお]して{くださいました}。
examples.en: My teacher kindly corrected my essay.

examples.jp: お忙[いそが]しいところ、来[き]て{くださって}ありがとうございます。
examples.en: Thank you for coming when you are so busy.

contrast.note: Same event, other subject. Superior + が goes with くださる; superior + に/から goes with いただく.
Same direction, plain level; for friends and family.
The opposite direction: from me up to the superior.

mistakes.bad: 先生[せんせい]に本[ほん]を{くださいました}。
mistakes.good: 先生[せんせい]に本[ほん]を{いただきました}。
mistakes.note: With the teacher marked に (the source), I am the subject receiving: that is いただく. With くださる the teacher takes が.

mistakes.bad: 社長[しゃちょう]がお土産[みやげ]を{くださりました}。
mistakes.good: 社長[しゃちょう]がお土産[みやげ]を{くださいました}。
mistakes.note: The polite form is irregular: くださいます, くださいました.

skills.tip: Check the particle on the superior: が means くださる, に or から means いただく.

skills.rule: When you or your side receive something from someone you respect, use いただく, with the giver marked に or から.
skills.explain:
いただく is the humble version of もらう. The receiver is the subject (usually 私, left out), and the respected giver is marked に or から. から is preferred when the giver is an organisation or when に could be read as the receiver.

With a て-form, ～ていただく means I had a superior do something for me, with gratitude built in: 先生に説明していただいた. Its potential form makes the most common polite request in Japanese: ～ていただけませんか 'could you possibly...'.

It is the same verb as the いただきます said before meals, where it is the humble 'eat'. The edge: いただく lowers you before the giver, so never use it for things received from your own juniors or children; that is plain もらう. And watch the particle: 先生が～をいただいた means the teacher received it.
patterns: (私は) [superior] に/から [thing] を いただく

examples.jp: 先生[せんせい]に本[ほん]を{いただきました}。
examples.en: I received a book from my teacher.

examples.jp: 先輩[せんぱい]にお土産[みやげ]を{いただきました}。
examples.en: I got a souvenir from one of my seniors.

examples.jp: 社長[しゃちょう]からお祝[いわ]いの言葉[ことば]を{いただきました}。
examples.en: I received words of congratulation from the company president.

examples.jp: 先生[せんせい]に推薦状[すいせんじょう]を書[か]いて{いただきました}。
examples.en: My teacher kindly wrote me a letter of recommendation.

examples.jp: もう少[すこ]しゆっくり話[はな]して{いただけません}か。
examples.en: Could you speak a little more slowly, please?

contrast.note: Same event, other subject: 先生がくださった = 先生にいただいた. Choose by whether the superior is marked が or に.
Same direction, plain level; for friends, family and juniors.
The opposite direction: I give up to the superior.

mistakes.bad: 先生[せんせい]が本[ほん]を{いただきました}。
mistakes.good: 先生[せんせい]が本[ほん]を{くださいました}。
mistakes.note: With が on the teacher, いただいた would make the teacher the receiver. When the teacher gives, use くださる.

mistakes.bad: 弟[おとうと]にお菓子[かし]を{いただきました}。
mistakes.good: 弟[おとうと]にお菓子[かし]を{もらいました}。
mistakes.note: いただく honours the giver; your own younger brother takes plain もらう.

skills.tip: Hands held out and head bowed: I am the subject, the superior gets に, the verb is いただく.

skills.rule: Use やる for giving to animals and plants, and in plain speech to your own children or younger siblings.
skills.explain:
やる is the downward counterpart of あげる: same direction (away from me), but it treats the receiver as below you. Its fixed home is feeding and watering: 犬にえさをやる, 花に水をやる. With your own children or younger siblings in casual speech it is also normal: 息子に小遣いをやった.

Many speakers now say あげる for pets and plants too (犬にえさをあげる); that is fine. The rule that matters for you is the other edge: do not use やる to a friend, colleague, stranger or anyone you should respect. It sounds as if you look down on them; only rough casual talk between close friends tolerates it.

～てやる does a favour for a junior (娘に絵本を読んでやった). Do not confuse giving やる with casual やる meaning 'do' (宿題をやる): the giving verb has a receiver with に and an object that changes hands.
patterns: [animal / plant] に [food / water] を やる
[own child / younger sibling] に [thing] を やる

examples.jp: 毎朝[まいあさ]、花[はな]に水[みず]を{やります}。
examples.en: I water the flowers every morning.

examples.jp: 犬[いぬ]にえさを{やった}？
金魚[きんぎょ]にえさを{やる}のを忘[わす]れた。
examples.en: I forgot to feed the goldfish.

examples.jp: 弟[おとうと]にお小遣[こづか]いを{やった}。
examples.en: I gave my little brother some pocket money.

examples.jp: 息子[むすこ]に自転車[じてんしゃ]を買[か]って{やりました}。
examples.en: I bought my son a bicycle.

contrast.note: Neutral outward giving. For pets either works; for anyone outside your own family use あげる.
Toward me. やる always moves away from me.
The top of the same outward scale; やる is the bottom.

mistakes.bad: 友達[ともだち]に本[ほん]を{やりました}。
mistakes.good: 友達[ともだち]に本[ほん]を{あげました}。
mistakes.note: やる to a friend sounds as if you look down on them; use あげる.

mistakes.bad: 先生[せんせい]にお土産[みやげ]を{やりました}。
mistakes.good: 先生[せんせい]にお土産[みやげ]を{さしあげました}。
mistakes.note: やる toward a superior is an insult. A teacher sits at the top of the outward scale: さしあげる.

skills.tip: If the receiver is a plant, a pet or your own child, やる fits; for anyone else, step up to あげる.
